source.text: National Master Bojo Jinul (1158–1210), Admonitions to Beginners: the first part of the Admonitions for Beginners (Chobalsim Jagyeongmun)
source.translationLicense: English translation and commentary: newly made by Sutra Box from its own Korean version (based on an AI draft, still being reviewed and refined)

g01.heading: One Who Has Just Set Out
g01.plain: One who has just aroused the mind should keep away from bad friends and stay close to the wise and good, receive and keep the five precepts, the ten precepts and so on, and know well what breaks them and when they are opened or closed. Rely only on the Buddha's holy words, and do not follow the wrong talk of the crowd.
g01.commentary: Master Jinul of Goryeo wrote this for those newly ordained. At the outset he lays the foundation of practice: good friends, the precepts and the right teaching. "Opening and closing" means judging when a precept may be relaxed or must be held, depending on the situation.

g02.heading: Living in Harmony with the Assembly
g02.plain: Now that you have left home and joined a pure assembly, always think of being gentle, mild and agreeable, and do not exalt yourself with pride. Treat those older than you as elder brothers and those younger as younger brothers. If there is a quarrel, reconcile both sides, treat everyone only with a compassionate heart, and do not hurt others with harsh words. If you deceive and look down on your companions and argue right and wrong, such a leaving of home is of no benefit. The harm of wealth and sex is worse than a poisonous snake; examine yourself, know your faults, and always keep away from them.
g02.commentary: This teaches the harmony to keep in a shared community. The basis of practice is a mind that cherishes others rather than one that wants to win over them.

g03.heading: Conduct in Daily Life
g03.plain: Do not enter another's room without reason, and do not pry into others' affairs in hidden places. Do not wash your underclothes except on the sixth day, and when washing your face and brushing your teeth do not blow your nose or spit loudly. When food is served, do not jostle or skip your turn; when walking, do not open your robe or swing your arms; when talking, do not laugh and chatter loudly. Do not go outside the gate unless it is important. If someone is ill, care for them with compassion; greet guests gladly; step aside respectfully for elders; and in providing your practice things, be frugal and know contentment.
g03.commentary: This shows that every small action is tied to cultivating the mind. Conduct that considers others is itself practice.

g04.heading: At Meals
g04.plain: At meals, do not make noise when drinking and eating; pick up and set down your bowls quietly and calmly; do not raise your face and look around. Do not like or dislike food for being fine or coarse, and keep silent to ward off stray thoughts. Know that you receive food only to keep the body from withering so you can accomplish the Way; recalling the Heart Sutra, see that giver, receiver and gift are all pure, so as not to stray from the Way.
g04.commentary: "The purity of the three wheels" means having no attachment to the giver, the receiver or the gift. Even a bowl of rice should be received with gratitude and awareness.

g05.heading: At Services and Recitation
g05.plain: Go to the services diligently morning and evening, and rebuke yourself for laziness; know the order of the assembly and do not disturb it. When chanting praises and blessings, reflect on the meaning as you recite, and do not just follow the sound or break the rhythm. When gazing up in reverence at the Buddha's face, do not let your mind wander to other things. Know that your karmic wrongs are like mountains and seas, and know they can be removed by repentance in principle and repentance in practice. Reflect deeply that you who bow and the Buddha who receives the bow both arise by conditions from true nature, and believe deeply that the response is never in vain, but follows like a shadow or an echo.
g05.commentary: Repentance in principle means realizing that the nature of wrongdoing is empty; repentance in practice means regretting wrongs through bowing and recitation. Form and principle should go together.

g06.heading: Living Together and Going Out
g06.plain: When living in the assembly hall, yield to one another without quarrel, and help and look after one another. Avoid winning and losing in arguments, avoid idle gossip with heads together, avoid putting on others' shoes by mistake, and avoid breaking the order of sitting and lying down. When talking with guests, do not reveal the faults of the house; praise only the temple's work. Do not go to the storehouse, see and hear its various affairs, and give rise to suspicion. Unless it is important, do not wander the towns befriending worldly people, earning others' dislike and losing the mind of the Way. If you must go out, tell the abbot and those in charge of the assembly so they know where you have gone. When you enter a lay household, hold firmly to right thought so that your mind does not drift after what you see and hear. How much worse to open your robe, laugh and chatter, speak idly, take wine and food at the wrong time and act as if nothing matters: this greatly breaks the Buddha's precepts. Standing where the wise and good would suspect you, how can you be called wise?
g06.commentary: This gives small courtesies for shared living and rules for going out. Practitioners restrain themselves not for others' eyes but to guard their own right thought.

g07.heading: Staying in the Meditation Hall
g07.plain: When staying in a place of practice, avoid going about with novices, avoid comings and goings for mere courtesy, avoid looking at others' good and bad points, avoid greedily seeking after words alone, avoid sleeping too much, and avoid letting the mind scatter and be pulled toward outer objects.
g07.commentary: Six things to guard against in a place devoted to practice. Warning against study that chases only words and against too much sleep shows well Jinul's emphasis on actual cultivation.

g08.heading: When Hearing the Dharma
g08.plain: When the teacher takes the high seat to teach the Dharma, do not think of it as a sheer cliff and feel like retreating, nor think it is what you always hear and take it lightly. Listen with an open mind, and there will surely come a time when awakening opens. Do not follow those who learn only words and try to be clever only with your mouth. As the saying goes, when a snake drinks water it becomes poison, when a cow drinks water it becomes milk; learning wisely brings awakening, learning foolishly brings birth and death. Also, do not look down on the one who teaches the Dharma; this creates obstacles on the Way so that you cannot advance, so be careful. A treatise says: when walking at night, if a criminal holds a torch to light your path and you refuse the light because the person is bad, you will fall into a pit. When hearing the Dharma, be careful as if treading on thin ice; incline your ears and eyes to hear its deep sound, calm your feelings and afflictions, and taste its profound meaning. After leaving the hall, sit silently and reflect; if anything is unclear, ask widely of those who awakened before you. Be careful in the evening and ask in the morning, so as not to stray by a hair. Only then can you be called one who has right faith and holds the Way in the heart.
g08.commentary: As the same water becomes poison in a snake and milk in a cow, the same teaching bears different fruit depending on the mind that hears it. The image of the torch, accepting the light of the teaching without blaming the teacher's faults, is famous.

g09.heading: Conclusion
g09.plain: The desire, anger and delusion ingrained since beginningless time are entangled in the mind; suppressed for a while, they rise again, like malaria that returns every other day. At all times, with the skillful means and wisdom of diligent practice, you must guard and protect yourself firmly. How can you idly waste the years in groundless talk and still hope to awaken to the mind's source and find the way out? Just make your resolve firm, rebuke yourself and do not be lazy; when you know your faults, move toward the good, repent and correct them, and make your mind supple. Practice diligently and the power of observation deepens; polish and refine and the gate of practice grows ever clearer. Always remember that you have met a teaching hard to meet, and your work on the Way will always be fresh; always feel fortunate, and you will never turn back. Keep on like this for long, and naturally meditation and wisdom will become round and bright, you will see the nature of your own mind, and in this illusory world you will use compassion and wisdom to save beings in turn, becoming a great field of merit for humans and gods. Strive, I beg you.
g09.commentary: Afflictions are like malaria: just when you think they are subdued, they return. So it ends with the plea that steadiness and keeping the beginner's mind matter most. It holds Jinul's core idea of cultivating meditation and wisdom together.

precepts.definition: The five precepts are kept by lay people: refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying and intoxicants. The ten precepts are received by novice monks and nuns.

three-wheels.definition: Knowing that giver, receiver and gift are all empty, and so not clinging to them.

repentance.term: Repentance in principle and in practice
repentance.definition: Repentance in practice is done through acts such as bowing and recitation; repentance in principle is realizing that the nature of wrongdoing is empty.

samadhi-prajna.definition: Samādhi (the mind gathered in stillness) and prajñā (wisdom). Jinul stressed cultivating the two together.
